title: Alpha School Speaks
author: Cognitive Resonance
summary: This investigative follow-up examines a new microsite Alpha School published, apparently in response to the author's earlier reporting on its AI-driven 'boot camp,' which lists 18 required 'life skills' including watching a full season of Survivor for 'critical thinking,' building a 100-follower social media audience, and undergoing biometric heart-rate monitoring while receiving critical feedback. The author quotes Alpha School's own justifications for each practice directly, then argues the common thread is a philosophy that treats every form of value as illegitimate unless reducible to a measurable KPI, replacing teacher judgment with metrics wherever possible. Beyond mockery, the piece raises a substantive concern: it questions whether the school's SAT score targets (a 200-point jump in eight weeks) are achievable without either AI-assisted test-taking or outright manipulation, given what it describes as a lack of underlying academic rigor. It closes with the author addressing Alpha School's own students directly, encouraging them to resist the program's metrics-obsessed culture while still expressing genuine personal warmth toward them.
points: Alpha School's own microsite frames watching Survivor, building a social-media following, and heart-rate-monitored feedback sessions as required 'life skills' with named metrics of success.
Identifies a consistent philosophy across the school's justifications: an objective metric is preferred over teacher judgment because it 'removes uncertainty' about whether a student truly succeeded.
Argues Alpha School's culture treats truth and value as contingent on having a measurable KPI, replacing subjective adult judgment wherever a number can substitute.

Raises a concrete academic-integrity question: an 8-week, 200-point SAT score jump for below-average students is not achievable through ordinary instruction, implying either AI-assisted testing or number-inflation.
The school's public defense of its practices arrived the same day the critic announced he was publishing his exposé, raising questions about the timing of its own disclosure.
quotes: The new microsite lists 18 specific "life skills" that students must complete as "prerequisites for the deeper, more advanced work ahead" — more on this later. Importantly, each of the boot camp activities I identified in my special report are included as required skills.

Our approach to social media is similar to our approach to AI. We do not believe that shielding students from a powerful technology that is essential to success in a modern world is a better choice than preparing students to use it well.

Most teenagers' default mindset is that criticism is evidence that something is uniquely wrong with them. If mastery depends on a teacher's judgment, a student can always wonder whether they truly succeeded. However, an objective metric removes that uncertainty.

One of the mindsets we aim to instill in our students is that when something becomes difficult, students do not see themselves as victims of that difficulty. We want students to understand that experiencing something that is difficult does not equate to being powerless, even if it initially feels that way.

I've corresponded with a few people who have some inside perspective on Alpha School and Joe Leimandt, the billionaire software-developer-turned-private equity-whatever-turned-"school principal," and it's become clear that for Alpha School, truth and value do not exist absent a Key Performance Indicator.

Unless they let kids use AI to take the test — and they very well might! — requiring a freshman student who scores a 1000 to jump 200 points within eight weeks...well I have many questions, because that is well-nigh impossible without cooking the books.
